parts.title: Does feeding zebrafish (Danio rerio) a lot help them breed better?
parts.abstract:
Abstract

The zebrafish (Danio rerio) is one of the most widely used animals in scientific research. In the past, people raised these fish in the lab with simple methods that came from home aquarium keepers. Some labs, though, need to breed a lot of fish and produce new generations quickly. For them, the approach has shifted. They now use methods, tools and feeds from commercial fish farming to help the fish grow faster and shorten the time between generations.

These changes have made labs more efficient. But we still do not understand well what happens when zebrafish eat food designed for a different purpose: to grow very different cold-water fish species quickly to the size they are sold at. To explore how this kind of heavy feeding might affect zebrafish, we took groups of young zebrafish (larvae) from two different wild-type lines, meaning two standard, non-mutant strains. We placed them in tanks at a standard density of 10 fish per liter. For up to 63 days, we fed them either a "high" or a "low" food diet. During their growth phase, the "high" food group received at least 8 times as many rotifers (tiny water animals) and at least 2 times as many Artemia (baby brine shrimp) as the "low" food group.

We measured growth, survival and breeding performance in these fish and in their offspring. By breeding performance, we mean fecundity (how many live embryos the fish produce) and viability (how many of those embryos survive). We found that fish fed more grew faster and could breed earlier than fish fed less. However, they were also more likely to produce a higher share of embryos that did not survive.
parts.introduction_first:
Zebrafish (Danio rerio) are now used more and more as a model animal for medical research. Part of the reason is that the ways of caring for them, and the technology used, have improved and become more refined. For some labs, a big part of this care is collecting thousands of healthy embryos for research, and doing it well and efficiently.

Early studies on how to breed zebrafish successfully looked at what happens in the wild [1, 2]. They also studied how males and females interact, and complex behaviors. These studies looked at the role of pheromones (chemical signals between animals) [3, 4], courtship behavior [5, 6], dominance [7], recognizing relatives [7–9], the harm caused by inbreeding [10–12] and how often fish spawn [13, 14].

More recently, studies have looked at other things that may affect breeding, linked to how zebrafish are domesticated and housed. These include how many fish can be kept in a tank [15], stress and infection [16], tools for collecting embryos quickly [17], diet and nutrition [18–22] and interruptions in the fish's daily body clock [23, 24].

Even so, breeding performance (fecundity and viability) may depend on a huge number of other, indirect factors, and many of these have not yet been studied. Things like comparing different generations, light intensity, water conductivity (how well the water carries electricity, which reflects how much is dissolved in it), age and growth rates are all likely to affect performance in some way. On top of that, in zebrafish facilities these factors are all connected to each other, and together they may affect whole groups of fish differently. So, to run any research operation as efficiently as possible, it is crucial to understand how important each of these factors is on its own.
parts.conclusion:
Conclusion

Many studies on how well zebrafish spawn say that diet and nutrition matter [27, 38]. Ours is the first study to give fish the same diet and nutrition but feed them in different amounts, so that they grow along two different growth curves. Even a well-balanced diet can do serious harm if it is fed in the wrong way. From these results, we now have a better view of how important feeding rates are in zebrafish nurseries, the tanks where young fish are raised. Feeding rates directly affect growth, as well as viability and fecundity, and in the end the health and lifespan of the whole group of fish.

The zebrafish community keeps gathering more data on how to manage fish so that they are healthier and perform better. There is still more to learn from the more refined ways of managing other fish species raised in the fish farming industry. One relevant example is how broodstock (fish kept for breeding) are managed differently from market fish of the same species [56]. For market fish, it is important to grow them quickly past a certain size, using food that the fish turn into body weight very efficiently. Broodstock fish, on the other hand, go through complex breeding programs. They are managed to produce as many offspring as possible, and to control that production, by regulating diet and nutrition, temperature and photoperiod (the daily pattern of light and dark) [57].

In most zebrafish research facilities, fish are mostly managed in the same way, whatever their purpose: the same temperature, water quality, photoperiod and diet. Perhaps the only differences in care linked to feeding show up across the fish's life stages (larvae, juveniles and adults). Our results suggest that a diet that makes fish grow faster may not necessarily be the best one for breeding.

Zebrafish care has already advanced a lot. The next big step should not be to make fish mature faster. Instead, it would help more to work out the diet and nutrition that produce the best eggs and sperm. That would let us better control zebrafish breeding cycles and get the best performance over the long term. In turn, this may help us define more precisely which conditions to adjust to encourage spawning, and to manage broodstock differently from a maintenance stock (fish kept to keep the colony going).
parts.introduction_rest:
We still do not understand well how growth, diet and breeding performance are linked in zebrafish, and scientists who work with zebrafish are still debating this question. Observations in the wild, along with detailed lab studies, have helped us learn what zebrafish need to eat [1, 2, 25–27]. Because of this, the diets used in zebrafish facilities have changed a lot over the past few decades.

In the past, zebrafish of every life stage were fed live food, such as Paramecium (tiny single-celled organisms) and Artemia nauplii (newly hatched baby brine shrimp), together with dry flake food [27]. Over time, this changed. Now diets are designed to match particular nutritional needs and particular life stages. For example, larvae are fed Brachionid rotifers (tiny water animals) [28], while juveniles and adults are fed ready-made commercial fish farm diets. On top of this, labs keep developing and improving their own diets. They do this with a method called cold-extrusion agglomeration, in which the food is pressed together into small pellets without being heated. This method gives a food that is more stable, easier to digest and better preserved [22, 29].

These changes have made zebrafish growth more flexible, and they have shortened the time between generations. Recent studies have reported faster growth using different numbers of fish per tank, different diets and different feeding schedules. With these, fish reached their first breeding at 57 days after fertilization, meaning 57 days after the egg was fertilized [28]. Aoyama [30] shortened this time further, to 47 days after fertilization. More recently, it has been cut even further, to 43 days after fertilization [31, 32].

Shorter times between generations are clearly useful for running a lab. But less attention has gone to whether growing very fast might harm breeding performance. In this study, we tried to control growth rates directly. We wanted to find out whether the speed of growth early in life might affect breeding performance, which we measured as viability and fecundity in zebrafish of the same age.
parts.methods:
Materials and methods

Ethics statement

Before we started, the Animal Care and Use Committee at Harvard University approved every experiment in which we used animals (IACUC protocol # 11–22). This committee checks that research animals are treated properly.

Animals (F0 generation)

The F0 generation is the first generation we studied, the fish we raised ourselves. We used fish from two wild-type lines that are often used in research, called AB and Tübingen. We set up a spawning event, which is a planned breeding session. For each line, we put 50 fish, 4 months old, into a separate breeding tank. Half were male and half were female, and a divider kept them apart so they could not spawn overnight. The next day, at 10 AM, we removed the divider and let the fish spawn for 60 minutes.

We collected the fertilized embryos from each line and moved them into petri dishes, 35 fish per dish, kept at a room temperature of 25.5°C. On day 5, we picked 420 larvae at random and spread them into 12 treatment tanks, each holding 3.5 liters. That gave 35 fish per tank, or 10 fish per liter. Six tanks held AB fish and the other six held Tübingen fish.

We checked the fish at different times, more often when they were very young. Each time, we picked 10 fish at random from each of the three tanks of the same line and moved them into small tanks measuring 9 cm x 16 cm, with 150 mL of system water. We photographed them from above with a Canon PowerShot S95 digital camera. We then measured each fish's standard length (the length from the tip of the snout to the base of the tail) on the photos using the program ImageJ (version 2.0.0-rc-69/1.52i). At the same time, we counted every fish in each tank to measure survival.

Dietary treatments, delivery (F0 generation)

Starting at 5 days post fertilization (DPF), meaning 5 days after the eggs were fertilized, we fed the AB and Tübingen fish two amounts of a rotifer called Brachionus plicatilis. This is a type-L saltwater rotifer, a kind of tiny water animal. We collected it from cultures that were kept going all the time, and we fed those cultures a diet of two algae, Nannochloropsis and Tetraselmis.

At 5 DPF, we gave every tank a first dose of rotifers: 155 mL at a salinity of 0.5% in tanks with no flowing water. After that, we added more rotifers every day, mixed into 50 mL of water at a salinity of 0.5%. Fish in the low food diet group (LF) received a first dose of 8,500 rotifers, and then on average 4,900 rotifers a day up to 11 DPF. Fish in the high food diet group (HF) received a first dose of 56,000 rotifers, about 6.5 times as many as the LF fish. From day 5 through day 12, the HF fish received on average 41,000 rotifers a day, at least 8 times as many as the LF fish.

While the fish were eating rotifers, all of them lived in tanks with still water. We did not feed them any extra rotifers on weekends (days 8 and 9 after fertilization). At 10 DPF, we put all tanks on a recirculating system, which keeps the water flowing around the tank, at 20 mL per minute (Fig 1).

Fig 1

Rotifer and Artemia fed to each tank each day.

(A) The amount of rotifers fed each day to each growth group, leaving out weekends (days 8 and 9). Open circles = LF, filled squares = HF. (B) The amount of Artemia nauplii (baby brine shrimp) fed each day to each growth group, leaving out weekends. Open circles = LF, filled squares = HF.

Once the tanks were on the recirculating system, we fed the fish two different amounts of Artemia nauplii (baby brine shrimp) from the Great Salt Lake, collected from cultures started fresh every day. Each day we hatched the same number of Artemia cysts (dried eggs), so both growth groups always got the same amount of Artemia. An automatic feeding system (Tecniplast) gave them the food. The HF fish started eating Artemia nauplii at 10 DPF, so for a while they ate both rotifers and Artemia. The LF fish started at day 12 after fertilization.

At first, the HF fish received about 8 times as many Artemia as the LF fish. As time went on, the HF fish received 2 times as many nauplii as the LF fish. As the fish grew older, we slowly raised the amount of Artemia for both groups. Until 60 DPF, the fast-growing group always got more Artemia (Fig 1B).

After the fish moved into their new, smaller tanks, we stopped feeding them all live food. Instead, we gave them two processed diets made for adult fish. Once a day, every fish got the same amount: on average 70 mg of a 60/40 blend of two fish foods, Gemma Micro 500 (Skretting, France) and Otohime B2 (Japan).

Time to first reproduction trial (F0 generation)

We wanted to know how long it took the fish to breed for the first time. We set up a breeding tank whenever more than half of the fish in a tank showed the body differences between males and females [33]. We then put all the fish from one tank of the three into a group breeding tank. We placed them in a special tank [17] that encourages zebrafish to breed, because it has shallower water, and shallower water has been shown to improve breeding in this species [17, 34].

We set up the fish in the evening. A barrier kept all the males apart from all the females, and they stayed this way for 20 hours, until 10 AM the next morning. Then we removed the barrier and made the water shallow, so the fish could spawn for 30 minutes. After that, we took all the fish out and put them back into their home tanks.

If the fish did not spawn, we set up the second tank of the three (tank B) for that line in the breeding tank, and it spawned the next day under the same conditions. We repeated this until the fish had spawned at least one batch of embryos. When they did spawn, we carefully collected the embryos from each breeding tank and placed them in a 1 L tank filled with 500 mL of system water. After 24 hours at 25.5°C, we counted by hand the total number of live and dead embryos, looking through a Leica M80 stereo microscope at 7.5 times magnification.

Spawning trials (F0 generation)

At 60 DPF, we picked five males and five females at random from the tanks of the high food diet group. We moved them into a smaller 1.1 L tank with recirculating water flowing at 125 mL per minute. This kept the number of fish per liter the same as in the tanks they grew up in. We did the same for the low food diet group at 63 DPF. During these moves, we kept the three tanks of each line apart, so no fish from one group ended up in another. Once the fish were in their new tanks, we gave them at least 5 days to get used to their new home before the spawning trials began.

From week 11 after fertilization, we set up all the fish to spawn once a week, in the same way as above. We put the fish in the spawning tanks by 2 PM, but a divider inside the tank kept males and females apart, so they could not breed overnight or as soon as the light came on the next morning. The next day, two and a half hours after the lights came on in the facility, we removed the divider so males and females could mix. The fish sat in shallow water and could spawn for 30 minutes.

When the time was up, we carefully took the fish out and put them back into their home tanks. Before turning the water back on, we weighed the fish. To do this, we moved all the fish into a 1 L tank with 200 mL of system water and placed it on a scale that had been zeroed (Ohaus, Model: Scout Pro SPE2001, Pine Brook, NJ). We netted the fish and patted them dry before weighing. We recorded these weights after spawning and then moved the fish back into their home tanks.

We collected the embryos from each spawning tank and placed them in a 1 L tank filled with 500 mL of system water, kept at 25.5°C. Twenty-four hours after each group spawned, we counted by hand the total number of live and dead embryos with the Leica M80 stereo microscope.

We used this method to set up each tank once a week for five weeks in a row, to copy how zebrafish are used in labs, where spawning can be demanding on the fish. After that came a five-week rest, and then we started spawning again for three more weeks.

Transgenerational effects

We wanted to find out whether feeding fish different amounts while they grew would carry over to the next generation. So we bred every tank of fish from the spawning trials to produce enough embryos to fill twelve new experimental tanks, six for each line. Each tank held 35 fish at 10 fish per liter.

We raised these fish to 90 DPF, by which time more than half of the fish showed the body differences between males and females. At that point, we picked five males and five females at random from each tank and moved them into a smaller 1.1 L tank with recirculating water flowing at 125 mL per minute. This again kept the number of fish per liter the same as in the tanks they grew up in (10 fish per liter). We gave the moved fish two weeks to get used to their new home before the spawning trials for the F1 generation began.

Dietary treatments (F1 generation)

At 5 DPF, we fed all the larvae the same type-L saltwater rotifer (Brachionus plicatilis). This time, though, the amount did not change: every tank got the same amount. The first dose in every tank was about 8,500 rotifers in 155 mL at a salinity of 0.5%, plus 300 μL of rotifer food. From day 6 through day 11 after fertilization, we gave about 4200 rotifers a day on average.

At 10 DPF, we put all tanks on a slow drip of a recirculating system (45 mL per minute). From day 10 after fertilization to day 90 after fertilization, we fed the same amount of Artemia nauplii in their first growth stage to all the young fish. On average, there were about 4200 nauplii in each mL.

Spawning trials (F1 generation)

At 104 days after fertilization, we set up the fish from both groups to spawn in the same way as described above for the F1 generation. In the spawning tanks, a divider kept males apart from females. All the fish spawned on exactly the same schedule as before: once a week for 5 weeks, then 5 weeks of rest, then once a week for 3 weeks. Twenty-four hours after each group spawned, we counted by hand the total number of live and dead embryos at 7.5 times magnification with the Leica M80 stereo microscope.

Statement of ethical approval

All the fish in the trials above lived in a 10,000 L recirculating system. The water always had a conductivity of 1250 μS/cm, a pH of 7.5 and a temperature of 28.5°C. At the end of the experiment, we killed all the animals humanely with a rapid temperature shock: we put them in system water at 2–4°C for at least 30 minutes, to make sure the gill covers stopped moving completely [35]. We used all the fish in this study in a way that was approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee at Harvard University (IACUC protocol no. 11–21).

Statistical analysis

Each spawning trial was a separate event from the weeks before it, so we treated each one as its own event. To compare spawning performance fairly within each week, we used a two-tailed t-test in the program GraphPad Prism v.5. A t-test checks whether the difference between two groups is bigger than we would expect from normal random variation. We called a difference statistically significant when p < 0.05. This means that if there were really no difference between the groups, a gap this large would show up by chance alone less than 5% of the time.

We measured spawning performance in two ways: fecundity (the total number of live embryos spawned) and viability (the percentage of embryos that were still alive 24 hours after spawning).
parts.results:
Results and discussion

Growth and survival of the parent fish (the F0 generation)

All the fish we used in this study survived well. We only had to make small changes to how crowded the tanks were, at 5 days after fertilization (DPF), just before moving the fish from petri dishes into 3.5-liter tanks.

We worked with two wild-type lines, called AB and Tübingen (Tü). In each line, fish fed the high food diet and fish fed the low food diet grew at almost the same speed. In the first 35 days, the low food group grew 0.44 mm per day (AB) and 0.43 mm per day (Tü). The high food group grew faster, at 0.74 mm per day (AB) and 0.75 mm per day (Tü). Over a longer period, up to 60 days, the high food group grew at 0.60 mm per day (AB) and 0.43 mm per day (Tü).

By 60 days, the fish in the two groups were clearly different in size, and the difference was statistically significant. We call a difference statistically significant when, if there were really no difference between the groups, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone. The number after "p" tells how rarely: p = 0.05 means less than 5% of the time, and smaller p-values mean even more rarely.

To describe the size of each group, we give the average (mean) length together with its standard deviation (SD), which shows how much the fish in the group varied around that average. At 60 days, AB fish fed the high food diet were 34.7 mm long on average (SD 1.3 mm), while those fed the low food diet were 26.3 mm (SD 1.6 mm). Tü fish fed the high food diet were 34.4 mm long (SD 1.2 mm), and those fed the low food diet were 26.4 mm (SD 1.2 mm) (Fig 2).

Fig 2

Growth of the two wild-type lines in the parent generation (F0), from 5 to 60 days after fertilization.

Average total body length of the two wild-type lines in the F0 generation, (A) AB and (B) Tü. Lines show the average ± standard deviation. Open circles = low food diet, filled squares = high food diet.

Breeding trials of the parent fish (F0 generation)

In most fish fed the high food diet, males and females could already be told apart by 40 days. Even so, we did not collect the first batch of embryos until 45 days, after the second attempt to get the fish to spawn. The first embryos came from AB fish fed the high food diet. These fish were 31.4 mm long on average (SD 0.78 mm) and weighed 0.26 g on average. We collected 14 embryos, and only 7% of them were alive.

The first embryos from Tü fish fed the high food diet came at 53 days, on the fifth attempt to spawn. These fish were 34.2 mm long on average (SD 1.07 mm) and weighed 0.30 g on average. This time we collected 171 embryos, and 57% of them were alive.

Most fish fed the low food diet did not start to look different as males and females until about 60 days. Neither group spawned until 63 days, which was their 8th attempt to produce embryos. AB fish fed the low food diet were 28.3 mm long on average (SD 0.82) and spawned 1092 embryos, of which 53% were alive. Tü fish fed the low food diet were 28.0 mm long on average (SD 0.85) and spawned 29 embryos, of which 62% were alive (Table 1).

Table 1

First breeding results of fish fed the low and high food diets.

Values recorded at the first successful group spawn of 35 fish. Fish were allowed to spawn for 30 minutes in total.

| Group | Days after fertilization at first spawn | Attempts to get embryos | Average body length (mm ± SD) | Average weight per fish (g) | Total number of embryos spawned | Viability (%) | Fecundity (number of live embryos spawned) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AB—high food | 45 | 2nd attempt | 31.4 ± 0.78 | 0.26 | 14 | 7 | 1 |
| AB—low food | 63 | 5th attempt | 28.3 ± 0.82 | 0.21 | 171 | 53 | 576 |
| Tü—high food | 53 | 8th attempt | 34.2 ± 1.07 | 0.30 | 1092 | 57 | 97 |
| Tü—low food | 63 | 8th attempt | 28.0 ± 0.85 | 0.21 | 29 | 62 | 18 |

By 11 weeks after fertilization, AB fish fed the high food diet had spawned 2749 embryos. That is more than twice the 1286 embryos spawned by AB fish fed the low food diet. In this first spawn, though, the share of embryos that survived was more similar in the two groups: 72% for the high food group and 76% for the low food group.

We also looked at fecundity, meaning the number of live embryos spawned. In the first embryos we collected, this was the only week in which AB fish fed the high food diet produced significantly more live embryos than AB fish fed the low food diet (p = 0.070). Over the eight spawning trials, the low food group had higher average fecundity in four of them. The difference was statistically significant in weeks 12 and 14 after fertilization (p = 0.001 and p = 0.011). Altogether, the low food group spawned 997 more embryos than the high food group over the eight-week trials.

In the low food group, the share of embryos that survived was higher in all eight weeks. The difference was statistically significant in four of those weeks: week 13 (p = 0.025), week 15 (p = 0.002), week 21 (p = 0.012) and week 23 (p = 0.031) (Fig 3A, 3B). The high food group's fish were heavier throughout the spawning period, but the weight differences were not statistically significant from week to week (S1 Fig).

Tü fish behaved differently from AB fish. By day 53 after fertilization, the total number of embryos spawned was more similar in the two diets: 739 embryos for the high food group and 666 for the low food group. However, the share of embryos that survived was poor in the high food group, at 40%, compared with 71% in the low food group. In seven of the eight spawning trials, Tü fish fed the low food diet had higher average fecundity than Tü fish fed the high food diet. The difference was statistically significant in weeks 13 (p = 0.008), 15 (p = 0.014), 21 (p = 0.030) and 23 (p = 0.038).

Over the eight-week trials, Tü fish fed the low food diet spawned 1879 more embryos than Tü fish fed the high food diet. The share of embryos that survived was also higher in the low food group in all eight weeks, and the difference was statistically significant in six of them: week 11 (p = 0.028), week 12 (p = 0.037), week 13 (p = 0.021), week 15 (p = 0.005), week 22 (p < 0.0001) and week 23 (p = 0.005) (Fig 3C and 3D). As with the high food group, the Tü fish fed the high food diet were heavier throughout the spawning period, but the weight differences were not statistically significant from week to week (S1 Fig).

Fig 3

Breeding results of the wild-type AB fish in the parent generation (F0).

Breeding results for the F0 generation: (A, B) the wild-type AB line and (C, D) the wild-type Tü line. (A) Fecundity is the total number of live embryos spawned. (B) Viability is the percentage of embryos that were still alive 24 hours after fertilization. Values show the average ± standard deviation. Stars mark statistically significant differences in a given week, found with a two-tailed t-test (a standard test for comparing two averages): * means p ≤ 0.05, ** means p ≤ 0.01 and *** means p ≤ 0.001. n = 3 means 30 fish from each feeding group.

After the breeding trials, we kept the F0 fish on the same feeding plan, feeding them once a day. At 7 months after fertilization, about 10 of the 15 F0 females from the high food group in both lines had swollen bellies. This suggested possible inflammation linked to eggs [36]. In fact, females fed the high food diet weighed 30% more (AB) and 45% more (Tü) than females fed the low food diet in either line.

We also tried spawning F0 fish in pairs. This worked better, gave more live embryos and gave a higher share of surviving embryos in the low food group. These results suggest that fish raised to grow more slowly can still breed better than fish that grow faster, especially once they are past the early stages of becoming adults.

Growth and survival of the offspring (the F1 generation)

As in the parent generation, all the fish we used in the offspring generation (F1) survived well. We again made only small changes to how crowded the tanks were, at 5 days after fertilization, just before moving the fish from petri dishes into 3.5-liter tanks. All the F1 AB and Tü fish grew at similar speeds.

In the first 35 days, all AB fish grew 0.41 mm per day. That is 0.3 mm per day slower than AB fish fed the low food diet in the parent generation. The Tü fish grew 0.40 mm per day, which is 0.2 mm per day slower than Tü fish in the parent generation. At 60 days, all F1 fish were smaller than the F0 fish at the same age, and they were far from becoming adults, because males and females could not yet be told apart.

We extended the growth measurements to 90 days, 30 days later, and found a total growth rate of 0.32 mm per day in both lines. By 90 days, the average length was almost the same in all four groups: 31.97 mm (SD 1.6) for AB, 31.63 mm (SD 1.9) for AB, 31.23 mm (SD 0.98) for Tü and 31.48 mm (SD 1.45) for Tü (Fig 4).

Fig 4

Growth of the two wild-type lines in the offspring generation (F1), from 5 to 90 days after fertilization.

Growth of the two wild-type lines in the F1 generation (offspring of the F0 fish), (A) AB and (B) Tü, from 5 to 90 days after fertilization. Lines show the average ± standard deviation. Open circles = low food diet, from parents fed the low food diet. Filled squares = low food diet, from parents fed the high food diet.

Breeding trials of the offspring (F1 generation)

The offspring generation showed no differences in breeding performance compared with the parent generation. F1 fish whose parents had been fed the high food diet spawned 13820 live embryos in total, while F1 fish whose parents had been fed the low food diet spawned 13076. The share of embryos that survived stayed steady from week to week. Averaged over the eight weeks, it was 87% (SD 7%) for the F0 high food group and 85% (SD 5%) for the F1 low food group (Fig 5A, 5B). Because both groups in the F1 generation ate the same diet, fish in the AB and Tü groups stayed similar in weight (S1 Fig).

Fig 5

Breeding results of the wild-type Tü fish in the offspring generation (F1).

Breeding results for the F1 generation: (A, B) the wild-type AB line and (C, D) the wild-type Tü line. (A) Fecundity is the total number of live embryos spawned. (B) Viability is the percentage of embryos that were still alive 24 hours after fertilization. Values show the average ± standard deviation. We found no statistically significant differences in either fecundity or viability. n = 3 means 30 fish from each feeding group.

The Tü zebrafish showed similar patterns. F1 fish whose parents had been fed the high food diet spawned 6931 live embryos in total, while F1 fish whose parents had been fed the low food diet spawned 7292. The share of embryos that survived also matched week by week, with no statistically significant differences. Averaged over the eight weeks, it was 65% (SD 9%) for the F1 high food group and 63% (SD 6%) for the F1 low food group (Fig 5C, 5D).

Comparing the share of surviving embryos in the parent and offspring generations

To see how the share of surviving embryos differed between the parent and offspring generations, we made a fold change comparison. For each line, we divided the average share of surviving embryos in the low food group by the average share in the high food group. A value of 1 would mean the two groups were the same.

In the parent generation, these values varied a lot and were far from 1. This points to clear differences in breeding performance caused by the different growth rates. In the offspring generation, the values were close to 1, with little or no change (Fig 6).

Fig 6

Fold change in the share of surviving embryos.

We used the share of surviving embryos in the F0 and F1 generations to calculate the fold change of the low food group divided by the high food group, in both wild-type lines: (A) AB and (B) Tü. Values far from 1.0 show a bigger difference in breeding performance.

In this study, we fed live food for the first 63 days after fertilization. Our aim was to find out whether feeding zebrafish different amounts changes how well they breed. Better feeding practices, improved diets and better management have all helped shorten the time between generations compared with what was first reported [37]. Here, we show how growth rates can be controlled without changing how crowded the tanks are, without making the water quality worse, and without removing the fish's natural daily body clock [31, 32].

Feeding zebrafish a lot has several benefits. For example, fish reach their first breeding and become adults sooner. But fast growth also has an unwanted cost for a zebrafish research lab: the fish breed less well, and the overall time window for producing embryos becomes shorter. On the other hand, slower growth, which can still produce adult fish by 63 days after fertilization, delays the time to becoming adults but leads to better breeding performance in zebrafish.

At the start of the breeding trials, fish fed the high food diet were bigger than fish fed the low food diet, both in weight and in length. The high food fish weighed 20% more than the low food fish and were 30% longer. The high food fish spawned first and even produced more live embryos in some cases (see F0 AB—high food, week 11). However, we also saw breeding performance drop over time in AB fish fed the high food diet, and drop even faster in Tü fish fed the low food diet.

More importantly, in 50% or more of the spawning trials, the share of embryos that survived was statistically significantly higher in the low food group than in the high food group. Fecundity was also statistically significantly higher in the low food group in 38% or more of the spawning trials (Fig 3).

It is well known that how well zebrafish breed depends strongly on their nutrition [38, 39]. Recent studies that report both growth rates and breeding performance show how the two are linked. Forbes [19] found that embryos from zebrafish fed until they were full, up to 28 days after fertilization, were smaller. Forbes also found a statistically significant link between the size of the yolk and the share of embryos that hatched. These smaller embryos later turned out to be of poorer quality and hatched less often than embryos from fish fed less.

In a study by Castranova et al. [15], eight zebrafish research labs took part together. The lab that noticed the difference between males and females fastest also had the lowest share of surviving embryos, no matter how crowded the tanks were. In another study, by Lawrence et al. [40], fish with the lowest average length and weight at the end of the feeding trials had the highest share of surviving embryos when they spawned. In the study by Monteiro et al. [22], fish fed a diet that made them grow fastest produced batches of embryos with a lower share of survivors than fish that grew more slowly. Newman et al. [41] studied how much underfed, poorly nourished fish ate, and found that better-nourished fish bred more successfully.

These studies did not focus on exactly the same questions as ours, but their findings support what we saw: diets and feeding plans affect how well zebrafish breed, and diets that make fish grow faster do not often lead to better breeding.

One possible cause could be the amount of essential fatty acids in the diet, or the lack of them [42, 43]. Essential fatty acids are fats that animals must get from their food. How much fish need them differs from species to species and depends on several factors [41]. Several studies have linked a lack of essential fatty acids to how often fish spawn.

Essential fatty acids control the release of prostaglandins, which are important as pheromones (chemical signals between animals), and they also affect ovulation in fish, which is the release of eggs from the ovaries. So, female zebrafish that do not get enough essential fatty acids from their diet may have a disrupted prostaglandin signaling pathway. In the end, this could stop them from releasing eggs, so the eggs can build up and break down over time [27, 43].

Feeding too much to make fish become adults sooner also seems to make their gonads (the organs that make eggs and sperm) develop faster [44]. Earlier studies have reported that in female zebrafish, the start of puberty depends more on body size than on age, and that fast gonad development goes along with fast growth [13, 45].

Yilmaz et al. [46] were the first to show which proteins are linked to egg quality in zebrafish. They used liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry, two lab methods that separate and identify substances. They found that poor-quality eggs lacked various proteins, including vitellogenin products, which stopped the eggs from fully maturing. In addition, in bony fish (teleosts), the germ cells that divide to make new eggs do not hold a limited number of developing eggs. Instead, they keep producing new ones throughout the fish's life [47]. In the end, the breakdown of developing eggs, called atresia, plays a major role in how many healthy eggs are produced [48, 49].

In our study, when we dissected large females carrying eggs, we did not find a sac full of eggs. Instead, we found fatty tissue, fluid from the ovaries and dead egg tissue, which often forms a plug that clogs the oviduct, the tube that carries eggs out of the body [50, 51]. This result may be explained by a mix of complex interactions between fats, the building of yolk (vitellogenesis) and the breakdown of eggs (atresia). Vitellogenin is a protein that forms the yolk. It is made mainly in the liver, carried by the blood, and taken up again and again by developing eggs [52, 53].

Zebrafish are classed as asynchronous spawners, meaning they do not all spawn at the same time. So eggs can be found at different stages of development at the same time [44, 48]. Vitellogenin has been found in every tissue except the intestines. When its levels rise, it does not build up in the liver but in the blood and in the belly cavity of zebrafish [54, 55].

How much fat the fish eat also plays a role in how many eggs they produce and how many survive. Zebrafish sit low in the food chain, so they need less food, which may affect how they use fats for energy. Fats that are not used may be stored in unusual places in the body, which may harm spawning. Fish do store some fat around the organs, under the skin and in the muscles [27], but this is small compared with the growth of the body and the ovaries [44]. Once the fish has reached a certain body size and become sexually mature, the body gives priority to the ovaries.

In our study, the weight of fish after spawning was not statistically significantly different between the two feeding groups. Females fed the high food diet may have put on weight mainly in their ovaries and in making eggs, as earlier studies have shown [27, 44]. However, the weight gain in fish fed the low food diet may have come from a mix of body growth and ovary growth. These factors speed up egg-making early on, but they may also lead females to make too many eggs and hold on to them as they age. This is seen more often in fish that are fed heavily.

We studied the offspring generation to find out whether the parents' diet would have an effect on the next generation. All F1 fish grew at the same rates as their parents on the low food diet. There were no differences in the share of surviving embryos or in fecundity during the 8-week breeding trial (Fig 5). Fish fed the high food diet spawned less well, but their offspring did not, at least when they were fed the low food diet. This suggests that the effects stay with the fish that live in those conditions and are not passed on to the next generation (Fig 6).

In both lines, the average share of surviving embryos and the total number of live embryos in the F1 generation were better than in the F0 generation. This gives even more evidence that feeding rates affect when zebrafish become sexually mature, the quality of their eggs and sperm, and how long they keep breeding successfully.
